# Unified Supply Chain Analytics - RFP Extract and Discovery Notes

## 1. Background

Harrow and Vale Distribution Group is a wholesale and retail distribution business operating 46 regional depots across the United Kingdom and Ireland.
We move approximately 9.4 million order lines per year across our wholesale and direct-to-consumer channels.
Today, order, inventory and shipment data lives in four disconnected systems and nobody in the business can answer "what is our true available-to-promise stock right now" without a manual reconciliation that takes two full days.
We want a partner to design and build a governed analytics platform that consolidates this data and gives merchandising, supply chain and finance a single, trustworthy view.

## 2. Current Systems Landscape

SAP ECC is our order-management and finance system of record, running on-premises, and generates roughly 40,000 sales order changes per day.
Salesforce Sales Cloud holds our wholesale account and opportunity data for the 1,200 trade accounts our field sales team manages.
Our warehouse management system is Manhattan Associates WMS, deployed across all 46 depots, and is the source of truth for pick, pack and stock-on-hand events.
Carrier shipment tracking arrives as EDI 214 and EDI 856 messages over SFTP from our three main carriers: DHL, UPS and a regional Irish carrier called Fastway.
A legacy Access-based spreadsheet process is currently used to reconcile SAP ECC and Manhattan WMS stock counts weekly, which the COO wants eliminated entirely.
We currently have no single inventory ledger; each depot manager keeps a local spreadsheet of "known good" stock adjustments.

## 3. Business Requirements

BR1. The platform must give merchandising a single, trusted view of available-to-promise inventory across all 46 depots, refreshed at least hourly.
BR2. The platform must eliminate the current weekly manual reconciliation between SAP ECC and Manhattan WMS.
BR3. The platform should let supply chain planners forecast depot-level stockouts at least two weeks in advance.
BR4. The platform must give finance a consolidated view of order value, margin and carrier cost by depot and by trade account.
BR5. The platform could support a future customer-facing order-tracking experience, though that is not in scope for this phase.

## 4. Functional Requirements

FR1. The platform must ingest sales order and order-line data from SAP ECC, including order status changes, at least every 15 minutes.
FR2. The platform must ingest wholesale account and opportunity data from Salesforce Sales Cloud daily.
FR3. The platform must ingest pick, pack and stock-on-hand events from Manhattan WMS in near real time across all 46 depots.
FR4. The platform must parse and load EDI 214 and EDI 856 carrier messages delivered over SFTP from DHL, UPS and Fastway.
FR5. The platform must reconcile inventory positions between SAP ECC and Manhattan WMS automatically and surface variances above a configurable threshold.
FR6. Supply chain planners must be able to build a depot-level stockout forecast using at least twelve months of trailing order history.
FR7. Finance analysts must be able to build margin and carrier-cost reports blended from SAP ECC order data and carrier EDI cost fields.
FR8. The platform should let merchandising build ad hoc dashboards in Looker without needing data-engineering support for every new question.
FR9. Data stewards must be able to see and correct records that fail data-quality validation before they reach reporting layers.
FR10. The platform must maintain a full lineage trail showing which source system and load run produced every reported metric.

## 5. Non-Functional Requirements

NFR1. The platform must support 40,000 SAP ECC order-line changes per day at peak, including the pre-Christmas trading period, without backlog.
NFR2. Depot-level inventory dashboards must refresh within 60 minutes of a source-system change during business hours.
NFR3. The platform must support approximately 350 named users across merchandising, supply chain and finance.
NFR4. Data-quality checks must flag any depot with more than a 2% variance between SAP ECC and Manhattan WMS stock counts within the same reporting cycle.
NFR5. The platform must retain transaction-level order and shipment data for at least six years to satisfy UK tax and audit requirements.
NFR6. EDI file processing must be idempotent so a resent or duplicate carrier file never double-counts a shipment.

## 6. Integration Requirements

INT1. Batch integration with SAP ECC for order, order-line and finance postings, using SAP-provided extract tables or IDocs.
INT2. Event-driven integration with Manhattan WMS for pick, pack and stock-on-hand events, ideally via the WMS's published event stream.
INT3. Daily batch integration with Salesforce Sales Cloud for wholesale account and opportunity data.
INT4. File-based SFTP integration to receive EDI 214 and EDI 856 messages from DHL, UPS and Fastway on a schedule agreed with each carrier.
INT5. The platform should expose a secure API so a future customer-tracking experience can query shipment status, though that build is out of scope now.
INT6. The platform must integrate with our existing Okta tenant for staff authentication into Looker and any data-steward tooling.

## 7. Data Requirements

DATA1. Order, inventory and shipment data must be modelled into a governed set of conformed dimensions (depot, product, carrier, trade account) usable across all reports.
DATA2. Data ownership must be assigned per domain: supply chain owns inventory and shipment data, finance owns order and margin data.
DATA3. Data quality rules must check for missing SKU mappings, negative stock quantities and orphaned shipment records on every load.
DATA4. Master product and depot reference data must be reconciled between SAP ECC and Manhattan WMS, since SKU codes differ slightly between the two systems today.
DATA5. Transaction-level detail must be retained for six years; aggregated reporting marts may be retained indefinitely.
DATA6. Trade-account data from Salesforce contains personal contact details for account owners and must be handled as confidential business data.

## 8. Security and Compliance

SEC1. All data in transit between depots, carriers and the analytics platform must be encrypted using current TLS standards.
SEC2. Role-based access control must restrict depot-level margin data to finance and senior supply chain roles only.
SEC3. SFTP credentials for each carrier must be stored in a managed secrets service and rotated at least every 90 days.
SEC4. An audit trail must record every manual data-quality correction, including who made it and when.
SEC5. The platform must support UK GDPR requirements for the personal contact data held in the Salesforce trade-account extracts.

## 9. Technology Preferences

TECH1. Our BI team has standardised on Looker for dashboards and would like the underlying warehouse to be BigQuery so Looker's native modelling layer can be used directly.
TECH2. We currently have no cloud footprint for analytics, so the delivery partner should recommend the supporting data-pipeline and orchestration services rather than assume Google Cloud is a given beyond the warehouse and BI layer.
TECH3. Our two in-house data analysts know SQL and Python; a platform that keeps transformation logic in SQL where practical is preferred.

## 10. Delivery Constraints and Timeline

CON1. The platform must be live and reconciling SAP ECC against Manhattan WMS before our pre-Christmas peak trading period begins, which the program sponsor has set at 30 weeks from contract signature.
CON2. Depot rollout should be phased, starting with our five largest depots by order volume before extending to the remaining 41.
CON3. Our data team can allocate one data analyst half-time to this program; the delivery partner is expected to own data engineering and pipeline build.
CON4. The legacy Access-based reconciliation spreadsheet must be formally retired within 90 days of the new platform going live.

## 11. Discovery Call Notes - 2026-08-27

Attendees: COO, Head of Supply Chain, BI Manager (Harrow and Vale); Engagement Manager, Data Architect (delivery partner).
The COO restated that eliminating the manual weekly reconciliation is the single most visible win the board is expecting from this program.
The BI Manager confirmed Looker is already licensed for 60 seats and the team does not want to evaluate an alternative BI tool.
The Head of Supply Chain flagged that Fastway's EDI feed has historically been the least reliable of the three carriers and asked for extra validation on that feed specifically.
It is still unconfirmed whether Manhattan WMS can publish real-time stock events at all 46 depots or only at the 12 depots on the newer WMS version; the BI Manager will confirm with the WMS vendor.
No decision has been made on whether historical data migration should go back three years or the full six-year retention window at initial load.

summary.text: The proposed solution architecture targets Google Cloud Platform (GCP) and is composed of 27 components covering 21 functional capabilities. It spans the full reviewed scope; see each component’s own rationale below for its specific citations.
summary.label: ai-interpretation

components.name: Web Front End
components.purpose: Serves the internal web experience and delivers static assets close to the staff who use it.
components.rationale: Firebase Hosting (global CDN) serves the web experience with edge caching, TLS termination and low first-byte latency worldwide. It addresses FR_01, FR_02 and FR_03.
tradeOffs: Edge caching improves latency but requires explicit cache-invalidation on release.
A globally distributed edge adds a small recurring data-transfer cost versus single-region hosting.
securityConsiderations: Enforce HTTPS-only delivery and a strict Content-Security-Policy at the edge.
Restrict direct access to origin storage so all traffic is served through the CDN.

components.name: API Layer
components.purpose: Exposes the solution's functional capabilities as versioned, governed APIs for the front end and integrations.
components.rationale: Apigee API Management centralizes authentication, throttling and request validation ahead of the application compute runtime. It addresses NFR_01 and SEC_02.
tradeOffs: A managed gateway adds a small per-request latency and cost overhead versus calling services directly.
API versioning policy must be agreed early to avoid breaking existing client integrations.
securityConsiderations: Apply request-rate throttling and payload-size limits to reduce abuse and denial-of-service exposure.
Validate and authorize every request against the identity provider before it reaches the runtime.

components.name: Application Compute Runtime
components.purpose: Hosts the backend business logic that implements the reviewed functional requirements.
components.rationale: Google Cloud Run runs the backend services with managed autoscaling so capacity tracks real traffic without manual intervention. It addresses NFR_01.
tradeOffs: Container-based hosting requires a build/release pipeline for every deployable service.
Autoscaling limits must be tuned against real traffic before go-live to avoid cost or latency surprises.
securityConsiderations: Run containers with least-privilege service identities and no long-lived static credentials.
Scan container images for known vulnerabilities before each release.

components.name: Primary Relational Database
components.purpose: Stores the core transactional data the application reads and writes.
components.rationale: Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL provides managed relational storage with automated backups, patching and encryption at rest. It addresses NFR_01 and SEC_01.
tradeOffs: A managed relational engine caps vertical scale; very high write throughput may need read replicas or partitioning later.
Schema migrations must be coordinated with application deployments to avoid downtime.
securityConsiderations: Encrypt data at rest and in transit, and restrict network access to the application tier only.
Apply least-privilege database roles per service rather than a single shared credential.

components.name: Customer Identity and Access Management
components.purpose: Federates sign-in, session management and multi-factor authentication for internal staff against the existing identity provider, rather than a new customer-style registration system.
components.rationale: Identity Platform federates sign-in, session management and MFA for internal staff against the existing identity provider, with no new self-registration flow to build. It addresses SEC_02.
tradeOffs: A managed identity provider constrains custom sign-in UX to its supported customization hooks.
Federating with an external identity provider (SSO) adds a dependency on that provider’s availability.
securityConsiderations: Enforce MFA for privileged accounts and require strong password/session policies for all users.
Log every authentication and authorization decision for audit purposes.

components.name: Monitoring
components.purpose: Tracks infrastructure and application health so incidents are detected before internal staff are blocked by them.
components.rationale: Cloud Monitoring aggregates metrics and dashboards with alerting thresholds tied to the availability and performance targets. It addresses NFR_04, SEC_04 and SEC_05.
tradeOffs: Alert thresholds must be tuned to avoid both alert fatigue and missed incidents.
Detailed metric retention adds a recurring storage cost proportional to system scale.
securityConsiderations: Restrict dashboard and alert access to operations and engineering roles only.

components.name: Centralized Logging
components.purpose: Centralizes application and infrastructure logs for troubleshooting and audit.
components.rationale: Cloud Logging aggregates structured logs from every service with a defined, policy-driven retention period. It addresses NFR_04 and SEC_04.
tradeOffs: Centralized log retention has a direct storage cost that scales with request volume.
Log content must be scrubbed of personal or sensitive data before it is retained.
securityConsiderations: Redact personal or sensitive data from log payloads before they are written.
Restrict log access to authorized operations staff and retain an access audit trail.

components.name: CI/CD Pipeline
components.purpose: Automates build, test and release of every service into each environment.
components.rationale: Cloud Build with Cloud Deploy runs the build/test/release pipeline consistently across development, test and production. It addresses TECH_01, TECH_02, TECH_03, CON_01, CON_02, CON_03 and CON_04.
tradeOffs: A fully automated pipeline needs an initial investment in test coverage to be trustworthy for production releases.
securityConsiderations: Require code review and passing automated security scans before a release can be promoted.
Keep deployment credentials scoped to the pipeline identity, never to individual engineers.

components.name: Infrastructure as Code
components.purpose: Defines every environment declaratively so dev/test/prod stay reproducible and auditable.
components.rationale: Google Cloud Infrastructure Manager provisions and updates cloud resources declaratively, so environment drift is detected instead of accumulating silently. It addresses TECH_01, TECH_02, TECH_03, CON_01, CON_02, CON_03 and CON_04.
tradeOffs: Declarative provisioning has a learning curve for teams used to manual console changes.
securityConsiderations: Store infrastructure state and variables in a controlled, access-audited location, never in source control in plain text.

components.name: Secrets Manager
components.purpose: Stores and rotates credentials, API keys and connection strings used by every service.
components.rationale: Secret Manager centralizes credential storage with automatic rotation and fine-grained access policies. It addresses SEC_03.
tradeOffs: Every service must be updated to fetch secrets at runtime rather than reading them from local configuration.
securityConsiderations: Grant read access to a secret only to the specific service identities that need it.
Rotate credentials on a defined schedule and immediately after any suspected exposure.

components.name: Key Management
components.purpose: Manages the encryption keys that protect data at rest across storage and database services.
components.rationale: Cloud KMS issues and rotates encryption keys with a full audit trail of every key-use event. It addresses SEC_01 and SEC_03.
tradeOffs: Customer-managed keys add operational responsibility for key rotation and recovery policy.
securityConsiderations: Rotate keys on a defined schedule and restrict key administration to a small, audited group.

components.name: Backup
components.service: Google Cloud Backup and DR Service
components.purpose: Protects stored data with policy-driven, regularly tested backups.
components.rationale: Google Cloud Backup and DR Service takes policy-driven, encrypted backups on a defined schedule with a tested restore procedure. It addresses NFR_04 and DATA_06.
tradeOffs: Backup retention has a direct storage cost that scales with data volume and retention period.
securityConsiderations: Encrypt backups at rest and test restores on a regular schedule, not only after an incident.

components.name: Network Protection
components.service: VPC Service Controls with Private Service Connect
components.purpose: Isolates backend services on a private network so they are not directly reachable from the public internet.
components.rationale: VPC Service Controls with Private Service Connect keeps service-to-service traffic off the public internet and restricts inbound access to approved paths only. It addresses NFR_04, INT_05, SEC_01, SEC_02, SEC_03, SEC_04 and SEC_05.
tradeOffs: Private networking adds configuration overhead when a new service or integration needs external connectivity.
securityConsiderations: Default to deny-all network rules and open only the specific paths a service requires.
Log and periodically review network access-control changes.

components.name: WAF / DDoS Protection
components.purpose: Filters malicious inbound traffic and absorbs volumetric attacks at the edge, in front of the public entry point.
components.rationale: Google Cloud Armor inspects inbound requests against managed and custom rule sets and mitigates volumetric attacks before they reach the application. It addresses NFR_04, INT_05, SEC_01, SEC_02, SEC_03, SEC_04 and SEC_05.
tradeOffs: Rule tuning is required to avoid false positives blocking legitimate traffic.
securityConsiderations: Enable managed rule sets for common web exploits and review blocked-request logs regularly.
Alert on traffic patterns consistent with a volumetric or application-layer attack.

components.name: Integration API Management
components.purpose: Publishes governed, versioned endpoints for partner and internal system integrations, separate from the product’s own front-end API.
components.rationale: Apigee API Management exposes integration endpoints with independent throttling, auth and monitoring from the customer-facing API. It addresses INT_01, INT_02, INT_03, INT_04 and INT_05.
tradeOffs: Running a second managed API surface adds a small recurring cost versus reusing the front-end API layer.
securityConsiderations: Require mutual authentication (API key or mTLS) for every partner system calling this surface.

components.name: Integration Service
components.purpose: Coordinates data exchange with the external systems identified in the reviewed scope.
components.rationale: Application Integration provides managed connectors, retry and error-handling policy for each external-system integration. It addresses INT_01, INT_02, INT_03, INT_04 and INT_05.
tradeOffs: Each new external system requires its own connector configuration, credential and monitoring setup.
securityConsiderations: Store integration credentials in the secrets manager and scope them per external system.

components.name: Message Queue
components.purpose: Decouples integration producers and consumers so a slow or unavailable external system does not block the application.
components.rationale: Pub/Sub (queue-style subscription) buffers integration messages with dead-letter handling so failed deliveries are retried rather than lost. It addresses INT_01, INT_02, INT_03, INT_04 and INT_05.
tradeOffs: Asynchronous delivery means consumers must tolerate eventual, not immediate, consistency.
securityConsiderations: Encrypt messages in transit and at rest, and restrict queue access to the integration service identity.

components.name: Event Bus
components.purpose: Routes near-real-time events between the application and external systems that require immediate synchronization.
components.rationale: Eventarc routes schema-validated events to subscribers with sub-second delivery for real-time synchronization needs. It addresses FR_01, FR_03 and INT_02.
tradeOffs: Event-driven synchronization requires each consumer to handle duplicate or out-of-order delivery.
securityConsiderations: Restrict event publication to authenticated service identities and validate event schemas at the bus.

components.name: SFTP / File Transfer
components.service: Storage Transfer Service with a self-managed SFTP gateway on Compute Engine
components.purpose: Exchanges files with external systems that only support batch file transfer rather than APIs or events.
components.rationale: Storage Transfer Service with a self-managed SFTP gateway on Compute Engine provides a managed SFTP endpoint backed by object storage for scheduled partner file exchange. It addresses INT_04.
tradeOffs: File-based exchange typically has higher latency and weaker delivery guarantees than an API or event integration.
securityConsiderations: Restrict file transfer accounts to the minimum directories required and rotate their credentials regularly.

components.name: Scheduler
components.purpose: Triggers recurring batch jobs such as scheduled data synchronization and report generation.
components.rationale: Cloud Scheduler triggers batch jobs on a defined cron schedule with built-in retry on failure. It addresses INT_01 and INT_03.
tradeOffs: Scheduled jobs need monitoring of their own to detect a silently skipped or failed run.
securityConsiderations: Run scheduled jobs under a dedicated, least-privilege service identity.

components.name: Data Warehouse
components.purpose: Provides a column-oriented analytical store for cross-domain reporting and analysis.
components.rationale: BigQuery holds curated, query-optimized data separate from transactional load so reporting never competes with production traffic. It addresses FR_06, FR_07, FR_09, FR_10, NFR_02, NFR_06, DATA_01, DATA_06, SEC_01, TECH_01 and TECH_02.
tradeOffs: A separate analytical store adds pipeline latency between an event occurring and it being reportable.
securityConsiderations: Apply row/column-level access controls so analysts see only the data domains they are authorized for.

components.name: ETL Pipeline
components.purpose: Moves and transforms data from source systems into the analytical store or between domains.
components.rationale: Dataflow runs scheduled extraction and transformation jobs with data-quality checks before data lands downstream. It addresses BR_04, FR_01, FR_02, FR_03 and TECH_02.
tradeOffs: Pipeline failures require monitoring and a defined re-run/backfill procedure to avoid silent data gaps.
securityConsiderations: Mask or tokenize sensitive fields during transformation before data reaches lower-trust environments.

components.name: BI / Reporting
components.purpose: Delivers self-service dashboards and reports to business stakeholders over the warehouse.
components.rationale: Looker provides governed, self-service dashboards over curated warehouse data. It addresses FR_06, FR_07, FR_09, FR_10, NFR_02, NFR_06, DATA_01, DATA_06, SEC_01, TECH_01 and TECH_02.
tradeOffs: Self-service reporting requires a governed semantic layer to prevent conflicting metric definitions.
securityConsiderations: Scope dashboard access by role so stakeholders see only their authorized data domains.

components.name: LLM Platform
components.purpose: Provides managed access to foundation models for the AI use cases identified in the reviewed scope.
components.rationale: Vertex AI (Generative AI / Model Garden) gives managed, guardrailed access to foundation models so AI functionality is not built on an unmanaged model endpoint. It addresses BR_03 and FR_08.
tradeOffs: Model responses are probabilistic; outputs affecting decisions need a human-review step (see AI solution approach).
securityConsiderations: Apply content-safety guardrails and never send unmasked personal data in a prompt without a documented basis.

components.name: ML Platform
components.purpose: Trains, deploys and monitors the predictive models behind forecasting, anomaly detection or recommendation use cases.
components.rationale: Vertex AI (custom training and pipelines) trains and serves predictive models with drift monitoring, distinct from the generative LLM platform. It addresses BR_03 and FR_08.
tradeOffs: Predictive models need a labeled training dataset and ongoing retraining as behavior/data patterns shift.
securityConsiderations: Monitor for model drift and bias, and restrict retraining access to the ML engineering team.

components.name: Cache
components.purpose: Reduces database load and read latency for frequently accessed data under high concurrent usage.
components.rationale: Memorystore for Redis serves hot read paths from memory so the relational database is not the scaling bottleneck under peak load. It addresses FR_04, NFR_01 and INT_04.
tradeOffs: Cached data can briefly go stale after a write; time-to-live and invalidation rules must be defined per data type.
securityConsiderations: Encrypt cache traffic and avoid caching personal data beyond the minimum required time-to-live.

components.name: Workflow Orchestration
components.purpose: Coordinates multi-step approval and workflow processes that span several services.
components.rationale: Workflows tracks each workflow step’s state durably so a partially completed process can resume after a failure. It addresses FR_07.
tradeOffs: Orchestrated workflows add operational complexity versus simple synchronous calls and need their own monitoring.
securityConsiderations: Enforce the same authorization checks at each workflow step as would apply to a direct API call.

rules.name: Driver effort
rules.formula: driver days = baseEffort[driver type][complexity]; complexity = reviewer override ?? AI suggestion
rules.description: Each scope driver is sized from the editable base-effort table. The AI only suggests the complexity level; a reviewer override replaces it and is marked user-set. A driver without a base-effort value contributes no days, is reported as a blocked scope driver and blocks the cost of its workstream and the ROM.

rules.name: Workstream base effort and complexity
rules.formula: base days = sum(driver days); complexity = round(sum(level x driver days) / sum(driver days)), Low = 1 ... Very High = 4
rules.description: A workstream is the sum of its drivers. Its complexity is the effort-weighted average of the driver complexity levels.

rules.name: Environment uplift
rules.formula: infrastructure days x (1 + max(0, environments - baselineEnvironments) x extraEnvironmentPct / 100)
rules.description: Environments beyond the baseline add effort to infrastructure drivers only. When the number of environments is unknown, no uplift is applied, the input is listed as missing and confidence is reduced.

rules.name: Productivity factor
rules.formula: likely days = round((non-infrastructure days + uplifted infrastructure days) x productivityFactor)
rules.description: The productivity assumption scales all build effort (below 1 is faster than baseline). Likely effort is rounded to whole days.

rules.name: Overhead phases
rules.formula: phase days = round(total likely build days x pctOfBuild / 100)
rules.description: Discovery and Architecture, Testing and Hardening, and Deployment and Handover are sized as configurable percentages of the adjusted build effort and staffed with the overhead role mix.

rules.name: Workstream confidence
rules.formula: High -> Medium (Very High driver, related open gap or question, outstanding delivery dependency, missing planning input) -> Low (critical unresolved gap or question on an affected input, or a blocked calculation)
rules.description: Inputs map to workstreams by driver type: integration readiness -> integration, data volume -> data, AI data availability -> AI, expected users / environments / target regions -> infrastructure, compliance scope -> security, delivery deadline -> timeline. Every reduction is listed as a confidence limitation. Overhead phases inherit the overall confidence.

rules.name: Overall confidence
rules.formula: Low if any calculation is blocked, Low-confidence workstreams hold >= 30% of build effort, or 4 or more distinct estimation inputs are missing; Medium if any workstream is below High or any input is missing; else High
rules.description: The overall level is weighted by effort so that one small uncertain workstream does not dominate, while blocked calculations and a largely unspecified engagement always do.

rules.name: Effort range
rules.formula: low = round(likely x (1 - lowPct / 100)); high = round(likely x (1 + highPct / 100))
rules.description: The range width comes from the confidence-spread table, so lower confidence widens the range instead of presenting unsupported precision. Totals are the sums of the workstream ranges.

rules.name: Role allocation
rules.formula: role days = likely days x sum(driver-type days x role mix share) / sum(driver-type days), in tenths of a day (largest remainder)
rules.description: Likely effort is split across roles with the role mix of each driver type, weighted by that type's days. Role days always add up exactly to the likely effort.

rules.name: Workstream cost
rules.formula: cost = sum(role days x role day rate); range = cost x (1 - lowPct / 100) .. cost x (1 + highPct / 100)
rules.description: A role with allocated days but no day rate, effort without a role mix, or a driver without base effort blocks the workstream cost and the ROM totals. No default rate is ever substituted.

rules.name: ROM commercials
rules.formula: subtotal = roundToUnit(sum(workstream cost)); contingency = roundToUnit(subtotal x contingencyPct / 100); ROM = subtotal + contingency
rules.description: Low, likely and high values are each rounded to the configured rounding unit and reported in the configured currency.

rules.name: Timeline
rules.formula: capacity = teamSize x workingDaysPerWeek; weeks = ceil(effort / capacity); build window = ceil(sum(build phase effort) / capacity)
rules.description: Discovery runs first; the build phases run concurrently and share the team; Testing and Hardening may overlap the last 25% of the build window but always keeps at least one week after it; Deployment and Handover runs last. The range applies the timeline confidence spread, rounded up to whole weeks.

rules.name: Deadline assessment
rules.formula: compare likely and high timeline weeks with deliveryDeadlineWeeks; required team = smallest team size whose likely timeline <= deadline
rules.description: When no deadline is configured the assessment says so, the deadline is listed as a missing input and timeline confidence is reduced.

rules.name: Missing inputs
rules.formula: missing planning input -> confidence reduced; missing day rate, role mix or base effort -> calculation blocked
rules.description: Each missing input names the affected workstreams or estimate components, the related scope items and how to resolve it. An input held open by a gap or question is never dropped: without a workstream of its driver type it affects the workstreams that share requirements with the open item, otherwise the overall estimate.

rules.name: Historical references
rules.description: Illustrative historical delivery references (sample data, not actual Topcoder records) are displayed for context only and are never an input to any rule above.

result.deadlineAssessment: The 30-week deadline is achievable: even the high end of the timeline range (23 weeks) fits, against a likely 17 weeks. The configured team of 6 is sufficient; the smallest average team that still meets the deadline at the likely effort is 4.
result.explanation: The estimate inputs for Unified Supply Chain Analytics Program are organised into 7 workstreams and 25 scope drivers across the build phases Experience and Core Platform, Data and Integration and AI Capabilities; Discovery and Architecture, Testing and Hardening, and Deployment and Handover are added as configurable overheads. Each driver cites the reviewed requirements, capabilities, architecture components, integrations or AI use cases that justify it, and its complexity is derived from the facts named in its rationale. A capability whose reviewed requirements are all already priced by AI use-case, integration or data drivers is priced once, in those more specific workstreams, never twice; two capabilities built from the same requirements are combined into one driver. The main complexity hotspots are Dashboards and Reporting (DRV_02), Core Platform Services (DRV_05), Audit Logging and Compliance Monitoring (DRV_06), Cloud platform foundation and environments (DRV_10), Performance and scalability hardening (DRV_12), General non-functional hardening (DRV_13), SAP ECC batch integration (DRV_14), Okta staff authentication for Looker (DRV_18), SAP/WMS product and depot master-data reconciliation (DRV_22) and Forecasting model: Twelve-month trailing stockout forecast (DRV_25). Security and compliance work is delivered through the named security capability in the functional scope, so no separate generic security workstream is planned; that would price the same controls twice. Only complexity levels are suggested here: effort, timeline and ROM values are calculated from the base-effort table, role mix, day rates, contingency and team size in the estimation configuration. Calculated effort is 455 to 696 person-days (likely 533) over 15 to 23 weeks (likely 17) with Medium overall confidence. The ROM commercial range is 429,000 USD to 656,000 USD (likely 504,000 USD) including 15% contingency. Every figure is produced by the documented calculation rules CR_01 to CR_15 from the visible drivers and configuration; none is generated by the AI.

executiveSummary:
This scoping package covers Harrow and Vale Distribution Group's Unified Supply Chain Analytics Program, grounded in 4 business objectives, 10 functional requirements and 6 non-functional requirements reviewed from the customer's own requirements text, alongside 5 integrations and 5 security or compliance requirements that shape the proposed solution.

Cloud platform: Google Cloud Platform (GCP); Requirement coverage: 100%; Effort estimate: 455 to 696 person-days (likely 533); Timeline: 15 to 23 weeks; ROM commercial range: 429,000 USD to 656,000 USD (likely 504,000 USD); Estimate confidence: Medium; Open questions: 3. 3 clarification questions remain open and should be resolved before this package is finalised. This summary and the estimates that follow are an AI-assisted planning output and require review and validation by qualified sales, architecture, delivery, security and commercial stakeholders before being shared with Harrow and Vale Distribution Group.
